item.title: CryoVault 2.0: Multi-Stage Vault Decryption & Coolant Pump Daemon Pwn
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{cry0v4ult_2_0_ch41n3d_c00l4nt_pump_pwn_c0mpl3t3}

1. Challenge Architecture & Engagement Scope

CryoVault 2.0 was the premier capstone infrastructure challenge of the ISFCR CryoVault Finals 2026. The target environment represents an air-gapped industrial cryogenic containment unit.

The architecture comprises:

  • Perimeter Supervisory Service: A TCP listener on port 9001 exposing the CryoVault 2.0 interactive operator shell.
  • Coolant Monitoring Daemon: A native x86-64 service listening locally on port 4141.
  • Acoustic Sensor Archive: An encrypted telemetry channel periodically saving sensory wave files (coolant.wav) into /var/log/cryo/.
  • FrostVM Execution Core: An obfuscated virtual machine interpreting encrypted operational directives.

The challenge objective is to penetrate the cooling control loops, pivot to the pump controller, and dump the master vault key from physical sector storage.

item.title: CryoVault Thaw Interlock (Firmware 4.3): P-256 Schnorr Seal Scalar Recovery
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{th4w_1nt3rl0ck_p256_schn0rr_sc4l4r_r3c0v3r3d}

1. Cryptographic System Overview

The CryoVault Thaw Interlock controller runs Firmware 4.3. To execute an emergency core thaw, the remote control console requires a valid Schnorr signature over the NIST P-256 elliptic curve:

$$s = k + e \cdot d \pmod n$$

where $d$ is the vault master seal scalar, $k$ is an ephemeral nonce, $R = k \cdot G$, and $e = H(R \parallel m)$.

item.description:

1. Cryptographic Structure & Weak Key Derivation

An encrypted backup archive was recovered from an abandoned corporate server. The decryption routine specifies:

  • Cipher: AES-128-CBC
  • Key: MD5(wordlist_password + 4_digit_pin)
  • IV: Fixed 16-byte header prepended to the ciphertext.

Because the password space consists of a common 1,000-word dictionary appended with a 4-digit PIN ($1000 \times 10^4 = 10^7$ total combinations), we conducted an exhaustive parallel padding oracle check in Python. The key was recovered in under 12 seconds on a single CPU core.

item.title: The Vandoria Leak — "Operation Nexus Gate"
item.description:
Captured Flag SoS{n3xtjs_m1ddl3w4r3_ssrf_n3xus_g4t3}

1. Application Architecture & Recon

The target web service is built using Next.js 14 App Router. Accessing /admin/nexus-gate returned a strict HTTP 403 Forbidden generated by middleware.ts:

export function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
 if (request.nextUrl.pathname.startsWith('/admin')) {
 const internal = request.headers.get('x-internal-loopback');
 if (internal !== process.env.INTERNAL_SECRET) {
 return NextResponse.json({ error: "Unauthorized" }, { status: 403 });
 }
 }
}

2. Vulnerability Chaining: Server Action SSRF & Header Mismatch

  1. Next.js Route Normalization Discrepancy: Next.js route matchers normalize URL path encodings differently between edge middleware and Node.js server actions. By requesting /admin%2f/nexus-gate or exploiting path trailing slash normalization, the middleware regex failed to match while the backend route resolved to the admin controller.
  2. Server Action SSRF: The public profile photo upload endpoint accepted a remote image URL. By specifying an internal loopback target pointing to http://localhost:3000/internal/vault, the backend SSRF fetched the internal secret header, allowing full bypass of the admin gateway to dump the flag.

item.title: The Last Astra - An Unprovable Command
item.description:
Captured Flag PINAKA{last_astra_unprovable_command_shattered}

Challenge

The service is an “Astra command desk” that fires an order only if both of two seals accept a submitted command against that order’s published syndrome:

  • Dharma Seal — checks 0 <= v_j < B and A·v ≡ t (mod p)
  • Rigor Seal — checks 0 <= v_j < B and A·v ≡ t (mod p2)

The sanction matrix is block-diagonal: A = I_m ⊗ (B^0, B^1, ..., B^{k-1}), so a command is a vector v of n = m*k bounded integers, and each register’s syndrome is just v read as a base-B number: t_i = Σ v[i*k+l] * B^l.

item.title: Matrix Keystream: Linear Cryptanalysis & State Reconstruction over GF(2)
item.description:
Captured Flag NR{m4tr1x_k3ystr34m_l1n34r_c0nv0lut10n_br0k3n}

1. Cipher Formulation

The challenge implemented a state machine running a linear recurrence over a $16 \times 16$ binary matrix $M$. The output keystream $k_t$ satisfies: $$k_t = v_0 M^t \pmod 2$$

2. Inversion Attack

Because the state transition is strictly linear over $\text{GF}(2)$, collecting 16 consecutive output vectors enables direct matrix inversion: $$V = [k_0, k_1, \dots, k_{15}] \implies v_0 = V \cdot M^{-1} \pmod 2$$ Using SymPy / NumPy binary Gaussian elimination recovered the seed key in milliseconds.

item.title: ECHO-9
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{echo9_b5f049f6b72f5bda5bd20acbc3b5b2f8a566}

1. Sensor Telemetry & EEPROM Reconstruction

Provided with EEPROM dumps and PCAP traffic for an industrial ECHO-9 environmental sensor. Reassembling the TCP streams isolated periodic telemetry encrypted with AES-CTR.

2. Keystream Cancellation Attack

The sensor firmware experienced an unhandled watchdog reset, causing it to reuse an AES-CTR counter sequence across a reset notification and a subsequent diagnostic response. Because the reset notification format is deterministic and known, XORing the known plaintext with both ciphertexts completely eliminated the keystream, disclosing the diagnostic flag.

item.title: end-mark
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{gl1bc_235_tc4ch3_p01s0n1ng_r00t}

1. Binary Protections & Heap Flaw

The binary runs under glibc 2.35 with full protections (RELRO, Canary, NX, PIE). A classic Use-After-Free (UAF) vulnerability allows writing to a chunk after it has been freed into the tcache bin.

2. Safe Linking Bypass & Exploitation

glibc 2.35 protects tcache pointers with safe linking: $$P’ = (L \gg 12) \oplus P$$ By leaking the heap base address, we inverted the pointer mangling and poisoned the tcache forward pointer to point to the __environ pointer and overwrite the return address on the stack with a one_gadget ROP chain, yielding an interactive root shell.

item.title: FlaGuard
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{p4r3nt_f1rst_d3x_1s_s0_m34n}

1. APK Decompilation & Static Analysis

Decompiling flaguard.apk using JADX-GUI:

  1. In com.cryovault.flaguard.MainActivity, the user input is passed to Checker.validate(input).
  2. Inspecting Checker.java, we find an obvious string comparison against a decoy flag: "isfcr{decoy_flag_do_not_submit}".

InputStream is = getAssets().open("theme.pack");
byte[] encData = is.readAllBytes();
byte[] key = deriveKey();
byte[] decDex = decryptPayload(encData, key);
InMemoryDexClassLoader loader = new InMemoryDexClassLoader(
 ByteBuffer.wrap(decDex),
 getClassLoader()
);
Class<?> realChecker = loader.loadClass("com.cryovault.internal.RealValidator");

The true validation logic is loaded dynamically at runtime via InMemoryDexClassLoader from an encrypted asset named theme.pack.

item.title: Ghosts in the Bulb
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{when_photons_and_seconds_both_carry_secrets_a7c3}

1. Network Traffic Characterization

We were supplied with a PCAP capture smart_home.pcap monitoring unencrypted MQTT traffic across 12 smart home IoT devices.

Filtering MQTT traffic using tshark:

$ tshark -r smart_home.pcap -Y "mqtt" -T fields -e mqtt.topic | sort | uniq -c
 952 home/bedroom/light/state
 1420 home/vacuum/cleaner/telemetry
 340 home/living/thermostat/reading

2. Dual Covert Channels

  1. Brightness LSB Steganography: The smart bulb publishes JSON telemetry {"bri": <int>, "on": true}. Extracting the least significant bit (LSB) of the 952 brightness values yielded a continuous stream of binary data. The stream decoded to an 87-byte Base85 container prefixed with GITB.
  2. Inter-Packet Timing Channel: The container was AES-GCM encrypted. Analyzing the packet timestamps of the robotic vacuum (which was docked and supposedly idle) revealed that inter-packet intervals were not constant, but varied in integer multiples of 15 seconds: $30\text{s}, 45\text{s}, 60\text{s}, 75\text{s}$.
  3. Mapping interval $(t / 15 - 2)$ to 2-bit symbols reconstructed the secret passphrase: KZ7WMQR3XB2H.
  4. Deriving the key via $\text{SHA256}(\text{passphrase})$ decrypted the Base85 container to reveal the flag.

item.title: implicit-twins
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{1mpl1c1t_f4ct0r1ng_0f_tw1ns}

1. Challenge Overview & Problem Formulation

The target oracle publishes two RSA public moduli $N_1$ and $N_2$ along with a ciphertext $C = M^e \pmod{N_1}$ where $e = 65537$:

$$N_1 = p_1 q_1, \quad N_2 = p_2 q_2$$

Both moduli are unbalanced composite integers:

  • Prime factors $p_1$ and $p_2$ are 1024-bit primes.
  • Prime factors $q_1$ and $q_2$ are small 256-bit primes.
  • Most critically, $p_1$ and $p_2$ are generated using a flawed PRNG that causes them to share their lowest $T = 530$ bits:

$$p_1 \equiv p_2 \pmod{2^{530}}$$

The network trace contains thousands of anomalous DNS queries directed to domain *.tunnel.security-labs.io. The subdomains encode hex-formatted payloads with sequence numbers and CRC16 checksums.

Filtering DNS TXT responses and reordering sequence indices recovered a multi-part Gzip archive containing an exfiltrated incident report and the flag.

1. Challenge Overview & System Setup

In standard post-quantum Ring-LWE (Learning With Errors over Rings) cryptography, security relies on the hardness of finding a small secret polynomial $s(x)$ given noisy inner products. Here, the target service runs in the polynomial quotient ring:

$$R_Q = \mathbb{Z}_Q[X] / (X^N + 1)$$

item.title: Oatmeal
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{5958fbb07efd243b}

1. Android ODEX Extraction

Analyzing oatmeal.apk, standard DEX decompilation showed a native method checkFlag(String input). The binary logic was stored not in a traditional .so library, but inside an optimized Android runtime blob base.odex.

2. Disassembly & Constraint Inversion

Disassembling the target function with Capstone revealed 24 blocks of 11 ARM64 instructions, each validating one character via cyclic bit-rotation and table lookup. Inverting the 24 independent constraints yielded the string art_image_took_the_cake!. Computing the 64-bit FNV-1a hash and XORing with constant 0xa55a96693c3cd2ad produced the flag.

item.title: One pound fish
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{p0lyn0m14l_h4sh_c0ll1s10n_m4st3r}

1. Rolling Hash Analysis

The challenge service implements a polynomial rolling hash to authenticate session state tokens: $$H(s) = \sum_{i=0}^{k} s[i] \cdot B^{k-i} \pmod M$$ with $B = 31337$ and $M = 2^{64}$.

2. Collision Construction

Because $M = 2^{64}$ is composite and power of two, difference vectors can be constructed algebraically using low-degree polynomials. Using meet-in-the-middle over 8-byte blocks generated valid collision strings that authenticated as the administrative session.

item.title: Palimpest
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{p4p3r_r3m3mb3rs_wh4t_1nk_f0rg3ts}

1. Challenge Architecture & VM Disassembly

palimpest is a 4KB stripped x86-64 binary compiled with Zig. It implements an internal virtual machine that evaluates a 160-instruction program.

Unlike static VMs, each instruction in the bytecode stream is encrypted with an adaptive rolling hash chain: $$K_{n+1} = \text{Hash}(K_n \parallel \text{RegState}_n)$$

item.title: Signed, but which original?
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{h4sh_3xt3ns10n_4nd_c4n0n1c4l_c0ll1s10n}

1. Signature Verification Flaw

The document signing portal verifies files using a prefix-MAC construction: $$\text{MAC} = \text{SHA256}(\text{Secret} \parallel \text{Document})$$

2. Hash Length Extension Attack

Because SHA-256 uses the Merkle-Damgård construction without HMAC enveloping, an attacker knowing $\text{len}(\text{Secret})$ and $\text{MAC}(m)$ can compute $\text{MAC}(m \parallel \text{padding} \parallel m’)$ without knowing the secret. Appending administrative privilege directives forged a valid signature, unlocking the flag.

item.title: The Aggregate Remembers
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{bls_r0gu3_k3y_4gg4g4t10n_f0rg3ry}

1. Aggregate BLS Protocol

The target consensus service verifies aggregate signatures over the BLS12-381 pairing-friendly elliptic curve: $$e\left(\sum \text{PK}i, H(m)\right) = e(G_1, \sigma{\text{agg}})$$

2. Rogue Key Attack

The registration portal did not enforce Proof of Possession (PoP). By registering a malicious rogue public key $\text{PK}{\text{rogue}} = \text{PK}{\text{target}}^{-1} + \text{PK}_{\text{attacker}}$, the aggregate public key canceled out the target’s key, allowing signature forgery under our own private key.

item.title: The deletion echo
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{3xt4_j0urn4l_un4ll0c4t3d_1n0d3_r3c0v3r}

1. Ext4 Inode Recovery

A cloud server’s critical directory was wiped using rm -rf. The disk image backup.raw was analyzed with debugfs and ext4magic.

2. Journal Reconstruction

Because the filesystem maintained a journal (JBD2), transactions containing uncommitted directory index blocks remained un-overwritten. Carving historical directory B-Trees recovered the deleted files and the flag.

item.title: The image that forgot
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{jp3g_pr0gr3ss1v3_sc4n_h1dd3n_c03ff}

1. Image Header Triage

Analyzing forgotten.jpg with JPEGsnoop revealed that the image is encoded as a progressive JPEG containing 14 scan segments.

2. Hidden Scan Carving

Between the 11th and 12th scan segments, an undocumented APP14 marker contained 1024 bytes of high-frequency DCT data that did not render visibly on screen. Extracting and decoding this segment unmasked the flag.

item.title: The Loom
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{2nd_0rd3r_r3v_c3ll_aut0m8}

1. Challenge Architecture & Static Analysis

The binary loom reads 32 ASCII characters (256 bits) from standard input, maps them into a 256-cell boolean register array $S_0$, and executes $T = 1{,}000{,}003$ transitions of a 5-neighbour cellular automaton.

The state update rule implemented in the core execution routine: $$S_{t+1}[k] = g(S_t[k-2], S_t[k-1], S_t[k], S_t[k+1], S_t[k+2]) \oplus S_{t-1}[k]$$

item.title: The Recurrence
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{p0hlig_h3llman_sm00th}

1. Binary Triage & Disassembly Analysis

The challenge binary chall is a stripped 64-bit ELF executable. Running checksec:

  • Arch: x86-64
  • RELRO: Full RELRO
  • Stack Canary: Enabled
  • NX: Enabled
  • PIE: Enabled

Inspecting the main function in Ghidra reveals that the program accepts 28 bytes of input from standard input and packs them into a 224-bit unsigned integer $k$.

item.title: the-press
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{r4ng3_c0d3r_b1t_3x4ct_y0!}

1. Binary Analysis & Algorithmic Triage

The binary the-press accepts an input string of length 32 and processes it through two distinct stages:

  1. Adjacent XOR Pass: Computes $t[i] = \text{input}[i] \oplus \text{input}[i-1]$ for $i \ge 1$, with $t[0] = \text{input}[0]$.
  2. Binary Range Encoder: The transformed 32 bytes are encoded bit-by-bit using an adaptive binary range coder (similar to the entropy coder used in LZMA/7-Zip).

The resulting 36-byte compressed bitstream is compared against a fixed byte array in the .rodata section.

item.title: Write Hole
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{p4r1ty_n3v3r_l13s_wr1t3_h0l3_r3m3mb3rs}

1. Incident Scenario & Disk Artifacts

We were provided with three 17 MiB raw image files (bay0.raw, bay1.raw, bay2.raw) extracted from a crashed 3-disk enterprise NAS appliance. The system suffered a sudden power outage during heavy synchronous database transactions, resulting in a classic RAID-5 write hole where parity and data blocks fell out of sync.

item.title: Zygote Conspiracy
item.description:
Captured Flag isfcr{tw1n_pr0cess_h4ndshake_mem0ry_0nly_9f23ac}

1. Dual-APK Architecture Analysis

Two applications (app_alpha.apk and app_beta.apk) declare android:sharedUserId="xyz.srspace.suite" and share identical signing keys. Each package holds a 32 KB binary asset half.bin.

2. Inter-Process Memory Carving

At runtime, the apps establish an anonymous file descriptor (memfd_create) exchange over UNIX domain sockets. The combined payload is formed by XORing both half.bin streams and decrypting via ChaCha20 with an HKDF key derived from the shared APK signing certificate. Decompiling the resulting in-memory DEX exposed the flag.
